::: {.callout-important}
## The sentence to leave with

**`break` leaves exactly one construct — the nearest enclosing loop or `switch`.**

Nearly everything that goes wrong this week is that sentence, not yet believed.
:::

## Code You Can Copy

Every program below was compiled and run before it was put here; the outputs are what
they actually printed. **Predict each one before you run it** — that is the exercise; the
typing is not.

### 1 · One decision, then two — `if` / `else`

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int n;
    printf("Enter an integer: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);

    if (n % 2 == 0) printf("%d is even\n", n);
    else            printf("%d is odd\n", n);

    return 0;
}
```

```
7   ->  7 is odd
-4  ->  -4 is even
```

Note the test is `n % 2 == 0`, not `n % 2 == 1`. For `-5`, C gives `-5 % 2 == -1` — so a
program that asks "is the remainder 1?" quietly calls every negative odd number *even*.
Lab 03's drill 02 warned you.

### 2 · Many decisions in order — the else-if ladder

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int age, price;
    printf("Enter age: ");
    scanf("%d", &age);

    if      (age < 5)  price = 0;
    else if (age < 18) price = 60;
    else if (age < 60) price = 150;
    else               price = 80;

    printf("price=%d\n", price);
    return 0;
}
```

```
3   ->  price=0        12  ->  price=60
30  ->  price=150      70  ->  price=80
```

**The order of the rungs is the whole program.** Each test is reached only when every test
above it has already failed, which is why `age < 18` does not need to also say
`age >= 5`. Now swap the first two rungs and run it again: an 8-year-old pays 150.

Two questions to ask of any ladder: *do my cases cover every possibility?* and *can two of
them ever both be true?*

### 3 · `switch`, where sharing a body is the point

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    char c;
    printf("Enter a lowercase letter: ");
    scanf(" %c", &c);          /* the space skips the leftover Enter */

    switch (c) {
        case 'a':
        case 'e':
        case 'i':
        case 'o':
        case 'u':
            printf("%c is a vowel\n", c);
            break;
        default:
            printf("%c is a consonant\n", c);
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```
e  ->  e is a vowel        k  ->  k is a consonant
```

A `case` with no statements simply **falls into the next one**. Five labels, one body.
Here that is exactly what we want — remember this page when you meet the next one.

### 4 · The same mechanism, now a bug

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int input;
    printf("Enter an integer: ");
    scanf("%d", &input);

    switch (input % 2) {
        case 0:  printf("Number is even\n");
        case 1:  printf("Number is odd\n");
        default: printf("Neither even nor odd\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```
10  ->  Number is even
        Number is odd
        Neither even nor odd

5   ->  Number is odd
        Neither even nor odd

-5  ->  Neither even nor odd
```

Three lessons in one run. **Without `break`, execution keeps falling through** — 10 is
even, odd, and neither. The entry point moves with the value, so 5 prints two lines.
And `-5` prints only the last line, because `-5 % 2` is `-1`, which matches no case at
all — *that* is why the `default` is there.

Add `break;` to the first two cases and run it again.

### 5 · `switch` on a character — the mini calculator

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    double a, b;
    char op;
    printf("Enter: a op b   (e.g. 6 * 7): ");
    scanf("%lf %c %lf", &a, &op, &b);

    switch (op) {
        case '+': printf("%g\n", a + b); break;
        case '-': printf("%g\n", a - b); break;
        case '*': printf("%g\n", a * b); break;
        case '/':
            if (b == 0) printf("cannot divide by zero\n");
            else        printf("%g\n", a / b);
            break;
        default:  printf("unknown operator '%c'\n", op);
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```
6 * 7   ->  42
10 / 4  ->  2.5
9 / 0   ->  cannot divide by zero
5 ^ 2   ->  unknown operator '^'
```

The `/` case carries an `if` inside it: dividing by zero is a **precondition** the
operator cannot check for itself. And the `default` is what turns a typo into a message
instead of silence.

::: {.callout-tip}
Try it with `int` instead of `double` and ask for `10 / 4`. You get `2`. Week 3 is still
collecting debts.
:::

### 6 · `break` and `continue` in loops — is it prime?

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int n, i, divisor;

    while (1) {                          /* keep going until told to stop */
        printf("Enter a number 2..99 (anything outside stops): ");
        scanf("%d", &n);
        if (n < 2 || n > 99) break;      /* leaves the WHILE */

        divisor = 0;
        for (i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) {
            if (n % i != 0) continue;    /* not a divisor - go to the next i */
            divisor = i;
            break;                       /* leaves the FOR, not the while */
        }

        if (divisor) printf("  %d is composite, smallest divisor %d\n", n, divisor);
        else         printf("  %d is prime\n", n);
    }
    printf("stopped\n");
    return 0;
}
```

```
97  ->  97 is prime
91  ->  91 is composite, smallest divisor 7
2   ->  2 is prime
-1  ->  stopped
```

**Two `break`s in one program, leaving two different loops.** The first ends the whole
session; the second ends only the divisor search. Neither reaches the other.

`continue` is the other word: it abandons *this* pass and goes to the next. Here it is
only for illustration — `if (n % i == 0) { ... }` would do the same job — but it makes the
shape visible.

Two things to try. Replace `i * i <= n` with `i < n`: still correct, and for 97 it takes
95 passes instead of 9. Then feed it `1`, and decide whether the program's answer is the
one the *specification* wants.

### 7 · `break` to leave early — three attempts

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#define PIN 4242

int main(void) {
    int entered, attempt, ok = 0;

    for (attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) {
        printf("Enter PIN (attempt %d of 3): ", attempt);
        scanf("%d", &entered);
        if (entered == PIN) { ok = attempt; break; }
        printf("  wrong\n");
    }

    if (ok) printf("access granted on attempt %d\n", ok);
    else    printf("access denied after 3 attempts\n");
    return 0;
}
```

```
4242              ->  access granted on attempt 1
1111 2222 4242    ->  access granted on attempt 3
1 2 3             ->  access denied after 3 attempts
```

This loop can end for **two different reasons** — the right PIN, or running out of
attempts. After the loop, the program still has to know *which*. That is the whole job of
`ok`: a loop that forgets why it stopped cannot report what happened.

### 8 · The trap — `break` inside a `switch` inside a loop

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    double balance = 1000.0;
    int choice, pass = 0;

    while (pass < 3) {              /* bounded so we can watch the bug and still stop */
        pass++;
        printf("\n1 balance  2 deposit  3 withdraw  4 quit\nChoice: ");
        scanf("%d", &choice);

        switch (choice) {
            case 1: printf("balance = %.2f\n", balance); break;
            case 4: printf("quitting...\n"); break;      /* <-- leaves the SWITCH */
            default: printf("not implemented\n");
        }
    }
    printf("loop ended after %d passes\n", pass);
    return 0;
}
```

Choose `4` — quit — three times:

```
quitting...
quitting...
quitting...
loop ended after 3 passes
```

**It never quits.** The `break` did exactly what it promised: it left the nearest
enclosing construct, and that was the `switch`. The `while` never heard about it.

The fix is not a cleverer `break`. It is to give the loop something of its own to look at:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    double balance = 1000.0, amount;
    int choice, running = 1;

    while (running) {
        printf("\n1 balance  2 deposit  3 withdraw  4 quit\nChoice: ");
        if (scanf("%d", &choice) != 1) break;      /* input ran out */

        switch (choice) {
            case 1:
                printf("balance = %.2f\n", balance);
                break;
            case 2:
                printf("amount: "); scanf("%lf", &amount);
                balance += amount;
                printf("balance = %.2f\n", balance);
                break;
            case 3:
                printf("amount: "); scanf("%lf", &amount);
                if (amount > balance) printf("insufficient funds\n");
                else { balance -= amount; printf("balance = %.2f\n", balance); }
                break;
            case 4:
                running = 0;                       /* <-- this is what ends the LOOP */
                printf("goodbye\n");
                break;
            default:
                printf("no such option\n");
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```
1               ->  balance = 1000.00
2, 500          ->  balance = 1500.00
3, 2000         ->  insufficient funds
4               ->  goodbye
```

## After Class

- **Type and run all eight.** Where the machine disagrees with your prediction, the
  disagreement is the lesson — find the rule you misapplied.
- **Break §4 further:** add `break` to `case 0` only. Now what does 5 print? And 10?
- **Break §2 on purpose:** reorder the ladder so an 8-year-old is charged 150, and explain
  in one sentence why.
- **Extend §5:** add `%` to the calculator. What must you change about the variables, and
  why does `%` refuse to work with `double`?
- **Extend §8:** add a withdrawal limit of 500 per transaction. Which construct does that
  belong in — the `switch`, or an `if` inside the case?

**Lab 05 is built on exactly this material.** The drills there will catch you on §4 and
§8 if you have not run them here first.
